sections.heading: 3 Theory
sections.text: 3.1 Notation and Definitions As in previous work, we assume two modalities that are embedded on the d d -dimensional unit hypersphere. Our embeddings are in the form of sample matrices 𝒳 ∈ ℝ N × d \mathcal{X}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} and 𝒴 ∈ ℝ M × d \mathcal{Y}\in\mathbb{R}^{M\times d} with modality means μ x = 1 N ​ ∑ x → ∈ 𝒳 x → \mu_{x}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\vec{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\vec{x} and μ y = 1 M ​ ∑ y → ∈ 𝒴 y → \mu_{y}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{\vec{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\vec{y} . Many downstream tasks rely on cross modal retrieval - finding the nearest neighbor of sample y → ∈ 𝒴 \vec{y}\in\mathcal{Y} among the samples in the other embedding 𝒳 \mathcal{X} by computing the ℓ 2 \ell_{2} distance between the two: NN ​ ( y → , 𝒳 ) = arg ​ min x → ∈ 𝒳 ⁡ ‖ x → − y → ‖ 2 \text{NN}(\vec{y},\mathcal{X})=\argmin_{\vec{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\left\lVert\vec{x}-\vec{y}\right\rVert^{2} . Since the embeddings lie on the unit hypersphere, the NN can equivalently be computed using cosine similarity. We focus on models trained with the multi-modal contrastive loss. During training we are given a paired dataset { x i , y i } \{x_{i},y_{i}\} (e.g. image and matching caption) and minimize the following loss: ℒ ( 𝒳 , 𝒴 ) = − 1 N ∑ i = 1 N log ℓ ( x → i , 𝒴 ) − 1 N ∑ j = 1 N log ℓ ( y → j , 𝒳 ) \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})=-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log\ell(\vec{x}_{i},\mathcal{Y})-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\log\ell(\vec{y}_{j},\mathcal{X}) (1) Where ℓ \ell contrasts an embedding with the other modality: ℓ ⁡ ( x → i , 𝒴 ) = e − ‖ x → i − y → i ‖ / τ ∑ y → j ∈ 𝒴 e − ‖ x → i − y → j ‖ / τ \ell(\vec{x}_{i},\mathcal{Y})=\frac{e^{-\left\lVert\vec{x}_{i}-\vec{y}_{i}\right\rVert/\tau}}{\sum_{\vec{y}_{j}\in\mathcal{Y}}e^{-\left\lVert\vec{x}_{i}-\vec{y}_{j}\right\rVert/\tau}} (2) with τ > 0 \tau>0 being the temperature parameter. We follow previous works [ 42 ] and define, for a paired dataset the local gap as the vector between a pair from the two modalities: g → i = x → i − y → i \vec{g}_{i}=\vec{x}_{i}-\vec{y}_{i} (3) We also define the global gap [ 11 , 42 , 27 ] as the vector between the modality means: g → = 1 M ​ ∑ y → ∈ 𝒴 y → − 1 N ​ ∑ x → ∈ 𝒳 x → = μ y − μ x \vec{g}=\frac{1}{M}\sum_{\vec{y}\in\mathcal{Y}}\vec{y}-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\vec{x}\in\mathcal{X}}\vec{x}=\mu_{y}-\mu_{x} (4) When the two modalities are balanced ( N = M N=M ), the global vector is the average of local vectors. Nevertheless, the global gap vector is well defined for any dataset consisting of two modalities, whether a bijective pairing exists or not. Figure 3 : Three points in each modality in ℝ 2 \mathbb{R}^{2} and the corresponding multi-modal contrastive loss along with the magnitude of the gradient of the loss. Lines connect true pairs. As long as the points satisfy relative alignment - the true pair of any point is also its nearest neighbor - the loss and the gradient magnitude are close to zero, even when there exists a gap. 3.2 Why Should a Global Gap Exist? Figure 4 : The evolution of embeddings using gradient descent on the contrastive loss ( Eq. 6 ) starting with two tight clusters. Both when using an unnormalized embedding space (top) and when constricting the embeddings to the sphere (bottom) they converge to a solution that has almost zero loss and for which a global gap vector exists and the gap vector is orthogonal to both modalities. We prove that minimizing the contrastive loss will lead to such a solution under certain assumptions. For full training details see Appendix H . Since the contrastive loss rewards embeddings in which the representations in the two modalities are aligned [ 34 ] , the presence of a global gap in embeddings learned using such a loss is highly surprising. Indeed, it is easy to show that the global minimum of the contrastive loss is obtained when the representations are maximally aligned, i.e. ∀ i : x i = y i \forall i:x_{i}=y_{i} , entailing no local or global gap, i.e. g → i = 0 \vec{g}_{i}=0 . But it is also easy to see that there exist many other embeddings that achieve almost the same loss as the globally aligned embedding. Figure 3 shows an example. The lines are the local gap vectors g → i \vec{g}_{i} which show the correspondence between the two modalities: ideally we want circles and crosses that are connected to lie on top of each other in embedding space, meaning g → i = 0 \vec{g}_{i}=0 . As can be seen in the figure, the loss and the gradient can be made arbitrarily close to zero without perfect alignment: as long as the corresponding embeddings are closer than all other cross-modal pairs, the loss and the gradient will approach 0 0 . In particular, the solution in the bottom right (where there is a modality gap) achieves practically the same loss and gradient magnitude as the desired, perfectly aligned solution. Intriguingly, gradient descent sometimes seems to prefer these low-loss solutions over the global optimum. Figure 4 shows dynamics of points in low dimensions, in which we minimize the contrastive loss with respect to the embeddings coordinates. In both of these cases, training converges to a solution that has almost zero loss but for which a global gap vector remains. Zhang et al. [ 43 ] postulate that dimensional collapse, i.e. when the embeddings’ variance within each modality is concentrated in relatively few dimensions, is the cause for the modality gap. But why does the modality gap happen when there is equal variance in all dimensions? Figures 4 and 5 show such cases - both embeddings are initialized by sampling from isotropic Gaussians, therefore maintaining equal variance in all dimensions even after normalization to the sphere. Still learning yields a representation with a global gap, even without dimensional collapse. Therefore, further investigation is needed. We begin by defining: Q x ​ ( i , j ) \displaystyle Q^{x}(i,j) = e − ∥ x i − y j ∥ 2 / τ ∑ j ′ e − ∥ x i − y j ′ ∥ 2 / τ \displaystyle=\frac{e^{-\|x_{i}-y_{j}\|^{2}/\tau}}{\sum_{j^{\prime}}e^{-\|x_{i}-y_{j^{\prime}}\|^{2}/\tau}} Q y ​ ( i , j ) \displaystyle Q^{y}(i,j) = e − ∥ x i − y j ∥ 2 / τ ∑ i ′ e − ∥ x i ′ − y j ∥ 2 / τ \displaystyle=\frac{e^{-\|x_{i}-y_{j}\|^{2}/\tau}}{\sum_{i^{\prime}}e^{-\|x_{i^{\prime}}-y_{j}\|^{2}/\tau}} (5) Which are known as the softmax of the logit matrix [ 20 ] . Q x Q^{x} can be thought of as a soft assignment matrix: for each x i x_{i} it measures the normalized affinity between x i x_{i} and all points y j y_{j} in the other modality while Q y Q^{y} does the same for each point y i y_{i} . By construction, the sum of the rows of Q x Q^{x} are equal to one, and the sum of the columns of Q y Q^{y} are equal to one. Using these matrices the loss becomes: ℒ ⁡ ( 𝒳 , 𝒴 ) = − ( 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N log ⁡ Q x ​ ( i , i ) + log ⁡ Q y ​ ( i , i ) ) \mathcal{L}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y})=-\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log Q^{x}(i,i)+\log Q^{y}(i,i)\right) (6) The gradient of the loss can be written: ∂ ℒ ∂ y i ∝ ( x i − y i ) − ∑ k = 1 N Q x ​ ( k , i ) + Q y ​ ( k , i ) 2 ​ ( x k − y i ) \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial y_{i}}\propto(x_{i}-y_{i})-\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{Q^{x}(k,i)+Q^{y}(k,i)}{2}(x_{k}-y_{i}) (7) The gradient has two opposing effects: an attractive force ( x i − y i ) (x_{i}-y_{i}) pushes y i y_{i} towards it matching x i x_{i} and repulsive forces which push y i y_{i} away from x k x_{k} . The strength of the repulsive force is determined by ∑ k = 1 N Q x ​ ( k , i ) + Q y ​ ( k , i ) 2 = 1 2 ​ ( 1 + S i y ) \sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{Q^{x}(k,i)+Q^{y}(k,i)}{2}=\frac{1}{2}(1+S_{i}^{y}) with S i y := ∑ k Q x ​ ( k , i ) S_{i}^{y}:=\sum_{k}Q^{x}(k,i) . Intuitively, this means that points for which S i y > 1 S_{i}^{y}>1 will be pushed away from the other modality (their repulsive force are stronger than the attractive force) while those for which S i < 1 S_{i}<1 will be pushed towards the other modality. Interestingly, points for which S i y > 1 S^{y}_{i}>1 are those that are close to the other modality ( Fig. 5 top), so gradient descent will reduce the variance in the direction of the initial gap vector ( Fig. 5 bottom). The following theorem formalizes this intuition. Theorem 3.1 . Let μ x \mu_{x} and μ y \mu_{y} be the modalities’ empirical means. Assume that ∀ i : ‖ y i − μ y ‖ ≤ ϵ , ‖ x i − μ x ‖ ≤ ϵ \forall i:\left\lVert y_{i}-\mu_{y}\right\rVert\leq\epsilon,\left\lVert x_{i}-\mu_{x}\right\rVert\leq\epsilon , and ‖ μ x − μ y ‖ ≫ ϵ \left\lVert\mu_{x}-\mu_{y}\right\rVert\gg\epsilon . Then the gradient of the contrastive loss with respect to the embeddings is approximately in the direction that shrinks the variance of each modality in the direction of the gap vector g → = μ x − μ y \vec{g}=\mu_{x}-\mu_{y} . Proof Sketch. We compute the Taylor expansion of k ( x ) = e − ∥ x − y ∥ 2 / τ 2 k(x)=e^{-\|x-y\|^{2}/\tau^{2}} around μ x \mu_{x} and use it to simplify Eq. 7 , yielding: ∂ ℒ ∂ y i ≈ − 2 τ ​ [ g → ⋅ ( y i − μ y ) ] ​ g → + O ⁡ ( ϵ ) \frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial y_{i}}\approx\frac{-2}{\tau}[\vec{g}\cdot(y_{i}-\mu_{y})]\vec{g}+O(\epsilon) (8) Thus y i y_{i} moved along the gap in the direction of μ y \mu_{y} . See full proof in Appendix A . ∎ Init. t = 25 t=25 t = 100 t=100 Figure 5 : (Top:) Two initial embeddings where the bottom embedding is color-coded based on S i y S^{y}_{i} . S i y S^{y}_{i} decreases with distance to the other modality. ( Bottom: ) The training dynamics of a toy model initialized with isotropic Gaussians. Training starts by shrinking variance in the direction of the gap according to Theorem 3.1 . Figure 5 illustrates Theorem 3.1 . The embeddings begin with equal variance in all directions, but training first shrink the variance in each modality along the initial gap direction g → \vec{g} , resulting in no variance in the gap. We now prove that once there exists a direction along which both modalities are constant, gradient descent will converge to a solution where both the local gap vectors g i g_{i} and the global gap vector g → \vec{g} are orthogonal to both modalities. Our result similar to that of [ 43 ] but it highlights the crucial role of double-stochasticity: convergence to a nonzero, orthogonal gap vectors requires that the two matrices Q x , Q y Q^{x},Q^{y} are doubly-stochastic , i.e. S j x = S j y = 1 S_{j}^{x}=S_{j}^{y}=1 . While both matrices Q x , Q y Q^{x},Q^{y} are singly stochastic by definition, only in certain point configurations will they also be doubly stochastic. One such case is when the nearest neighbor matching between the two sets is a perfect match so each x i x_{i} is assigned to exactly one y j y_{j} and vice versa. Empirically, we have found that in the later stages of gradient descent, double stochasticity does indeed hold approximately but this is not true in the initial iterations ( Fig. 6 left). Theorem 3.2 . Assume that at a given iteration t t there exists a direction v → \vec{v} such that ∀ x → i ∈ 𝒳 : v → T ​ x → i = a \forall\vec{x}_{i}\in\mathcal{X}:\vec{v}^{T}\vec{x}_{i}=a and ∀ y → i ∈ 𝒴 : v → T ​ y → i = b \forall\vec{y}_{i}\in\mathcal{Y}:\vec{v}^{T}\vec{y}_{i}=b . Assume that for all iterations after t t the matrices Q x , Q y Q^{x},Q^{y} are doubly stochastic. Then gradient descent on the contrastive loss ( Eq. 6 ) will converge to a solution where all the local gap vectors are the same g → i = g → \vec{g}_{i}=\vec{g} and furthermore, g → i \vec{g}_{i} and g → \vec{g} are orthogonal to both X X and Y Y . Proof Sketch. By the assumption that v T ​ x i = a v^{T}x_{i}=a for all x i x_{i} and v T ​ y j = b v^{T}y_{j}=b for all y j y_{j} we see that using Eq. 7 : v T ​ ∂ ℒ ∂ y i \displaystyle v^{T}\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial y_{i}} ∝ \displaystyle\propto v T ​ ( x i − y i ) \displaystyle v^{T}\left(x_{i}-y_{i}\right) − v T ∑ k = 1 N Q x ​ ( k , i ) + Q y ​ ( k , i ) 2 ( x k − y i ) \displaystyle-v^{T}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\frac{Q^{x}(k,i)+Q^{y}(k,i)}{2}(x_{k}-y_{i}) = \displaystyle= 0 \displaystyle 0 where the last equality used the assumption of double stochasticity. This means that gradient descent will not change the values of either modality in direction v → \vec{v} and hence will converge to a solution in which this direction is unchanged and in all other directions u → \vec{u} , the modalities will be perfectly aligned u → T ​ x i = u → T ​ y i \vec{u}^{T}x_{i}=\vec{u}^{T}y_{i} . ∎ Together, Theorem 3.1 and Theorem 3.2 explain the dynamics seen in Fig. 4 . At first, according to Theorem 3.1 , learning begins by shrinking the variance in the direction of the gap. Once this happens and there is no variance in the direction of the gap, then according to Theorem 3.2 the gradient in the vertical dimension of the top figure remains zero and the loss continues to decrease by moving the points only in the horizontal direction until the loss reaches a value close to zero with a constant, orthogonal gap vector. In the bottom figure, the initial iterations reduces the variance in the gap direction and subsequent iterations decrease while moving in the other two directions. This phenomenon of an orthogonal gap has previously been noticed to hold empirically for multi-modal models trained on various datatypes [ 42 ] . We term this the global orthogonality assumption and formally define it as: Assumption 3.3 . The gap vector g → \vec{g} is orthogonal to the affine subspaces defined by 𝒳 \mathcal{X} and 𝒴 \mathcal{Y} : ∀ x ∈ 𝒳 , y ∈ 𝒴 : cos ⁡ ( x − μ x , g → ) \displaystyle\forall x\in\mathcal{X},y\in\mathcal{Y}:\cos\left(x-\mu_{x},\vec{g}\right) = cos ⁡ ( y − μ y , g → ) = 0 \displaystyle=\cos\left(y-\mu_{y},\vec{g}\right)=0 (9) Our theorems provide an explanation for the origin of assumption 3.3 provided that the initialization of the two modalities takes the form of two, separated and concentrated clusters. Figure 6 (right) shows that this is indeed the case - the distance between the two modalities is much larger than the inner modality distance for random initializations of CLIP on real data. This has already been shown to be the case for multi-modal models, a phenomenon termed the "cone effect" [ 11 ] . To summarize, multi-modal models are commonly initialized in non-intersecting tight clusters with an existing gap. According to our analysis, under these conditions initial training dynamics decrease the variance of these clusters in the direction of the initial gap, while subsequent iterations maintain the gap while aligning the two modalities only in directions orthogonal to the gap, thus creating global orthogonality at convergence. For completeness, we provide more empirical support for our assumptions in Appendix D and further discussion of the dimensionality collapse assumption in Appendix C . Figure 6 : Empirical evidence for the assumptions of our thoeorems on training dynamics Left : The variance of S i x , S i y S_{i}^{x},S_{i}^{y} in log scale throughout training of Fig. 5 . The values of S i x S_{i}^{x} and S i y S_{i}^{y} approach their means as training progresses, which is 1 1 by definition, meaning that the matrices Q x , Q y Q^{x},Q^{y} are approximately doubly-stochastic. Right : KDE plot of the gap’s norm and the distances between the embeddings and their means calculated over 50 random initializations of CLIP (ViT-B-32) on 5000 randomly sampled images and texts from the Flickr30k dataset [ 10 ] . The within modality distance is much smaller than the distance between the modalities. 3.3 The Modality Gap Decreases Robustness We define robustness ("Rob") as the probability that when adding noise sampled from some distribution 𝒫 \mathcal{P} to the embeddings of modality 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , the nearest neighbor of some y ∈ 𝒴 y\in\mathcal{Y} will not change: Rob ​ ( 𝒳 , 𝒴 , 𝒫 ) = 𝔼 y ∼ 𝒴 , ϵ ∼ 𝒫 ​ [ 𝟙 OPEN NN ​ y , 𝒳 ) = NN ​ ( y , 𝒳 + ϵ ) ] \text{Rob}(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{Y},\mathcal{P})=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\mathcal{Y},\epsilon\sim\mathcal{P}}\left[\mathds{1}_{\text{NN}y,\mathcal{X})=\text{NN}(y,\mathcal{X}+\epsilon)}\right] (10) Notice that in the zero shot classification setting, this definition of robustness captures semantically meaningful changes - any change of nearest neighbor from image embedding to text, necessarily changes the classification of that image. We now ask how does the existence of the gap relate to the robustness of the models to noise in the embedding space. Figure 7 provides intuition. In this figure, there are two captions and the space of images that are close to one caption or another is defined by a linear decision boundary. Any noise added to the text embeddings changes the decision boundary between the two classes. In the case of a gap between the cluster of image embeddings and text embeddings, as images are further away from the texts, their sensitivity to change in the classification decision boundary grows. We prove this formally in the following theorem. Theorem 3.4 . Let { y → i } \{\vec{y}_{i}\} be a set of points in one modality (e.g. an image embedding) and x → 1 , x → 2 ∈ 𝒳 \vec{x}_{1},\vec{x}_{2}\in\mathcal{X} two vectors in the second modality (e.g. captions) with mean μ x = x → 1 + x → 2 2 \mu_{x}=\frac{\vec{x}_{1}+\vec{x}_{2}}{2} . Assume x → 1 \vec{x}_{1} is the nearest neighbor of some y → \vec{y} in 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . Under the orthogonality assumption 3.3 , moving any point y → \vec{y} towards the other modality by a global translation g → = μ y − μ x \vec{g}=\mu_{y}-\mu_{x} increases robustness: the probability that the nearest neighbor of y → \vec{y} in 𝒳 \mathcal{X} does not change after adding noise to 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , with covariance σ 2 ​ I \sigma^{2}I and zero empirical mean. Proof Sketch. The proof follows the intuition presented in Fig. 7 - as the query vector y → \vec{y} is closer to modality 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , a larger rotation of the separating hyperplane is required to decrease robustness. Therefore the theorem holds as subtracting the global gap vector decreases the distance between y → \vec{y} and 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . ∎ For full proof and generalization for the cases of | 𝒳 | > 2 |\mathcal{X}|>2 and general noise we refer the reader to Appendix A . Theorem 3.4 proves that under the orthogonality assumption, when moving one modality towards the other by translating it with the global gap vector then the embedding spaces become more robust and less sensitive to noise. This provides us with clear motivation to close the gap. We note that while the theorem is phrased in terms of the global gap vector, any vector that is orthogonal to modality 𝒳 \mathcal{X} will suffice, as long as translating y → \vec{y} with it will decrease the distance between y → \vec{y} and the mean of modality 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . Figure 7 : Illustration of the relationship between robustness and the modality gap. Two image embeddings (blue squares) are classified identically when using the black texts. However, once slight noise is added to the texts (red), only the image with a smaller "gap" will maintain its classification. In real applications, robustness is not the only desirable property of a system and a method that increases robustness while significantly decreasing the clean accuracy, will be of limited interest. We therefore strive to understand when does closing the gap have no effect on downstream performance, therefore solely improving robustness. Since most downstream tasks such as zero shot classification or text to image retrieval are based on cross modal nearest neighbors, we ask when can we guarantee that the nearest neighbors will not change when varying the gap. Theorem 3.5 . As in Theorem 3.4 , let v → \vec{v} be some vector that is orthogonal to the affine subspace containing the modality 𝒳 \mathcal{X} . Then translating the embeddings of modality 𝒳 \mathcal{X} by α ⋅ v → \alpha\cdot\vec{v} for any α ∈ ℝ \alpha\in\mathbb{R} , such that ∀ x i ∈ 𝒳 : x i ← x i + α ⋅ v → \forall x_{i}\in\mathcal{X}:x_{i}\leftarrow x_{i}+\alpha\cdot\vec{v} , does not change the nearest neighbor of y → \vec{y} in 𝒳 \mathcal{X} for any y → ∈ 𝒴 \vec{y}\in\mathcal{Y} . Proof Sketch. Since the vector v → \vec{v} is orthogonal to 𝒳 \mathcal{X} , the variance of modality 𝒳 \mathcal{X} in v → \vec{v} is zero, therefore moving 𝒳 \mathcal{X} by α ⋅ v → \alpha\cdot\vec{v} changes the distance from any y → ∈ 𝒴 \vec{y}\in\mathcal{Y} to all x → ∈ 𝒳 \vec{x}\in\mathcal{X} by the same constant, meaning cross modal nearest neighbors are preserved. For full proof see Appendix A . ∎ Under the orthogonality assumption 3.3 such a nearest neighbor preserving direction is simply the gap vector g → \vec{g} . Therefore Theorem 3.5 ensures us that narrowing the gap along this direction would not change performance of the model on downstream tasks such as zero shot classification.

sections.heading: 4 Algorithm
sections.text: From Sec. 3 we conclude that although the contrastive loss maintains the gap created at initialization throughout the training, it is desirable to close the gap in order to improve robustness. Theorems 3.4 and 3.5 provide us with a tool to do so - move the modalities towards each other along the global gap vector, as under assumption 3.3 this provably does not affect performance on downstream tasks when there is no noise at all. Since in practice the gap vector is not completely orthogonal to the modality subspaces (see Appendix D ), we suggest projecting the gap vector to be exactly orthogonal to the affine subspace of the modality being retrieved before closing the gap. This is done by computing the principal components V V of the modality being retrieved (texts in case of classification) and projecting the gap g → \vec{g} to the orthogonal complement of the components: g → ′ ← g → − V ​ V T ​ g → \vec{g}^{\prime}\leftarrow\vec{g}-VV^{T}\vec{g} (11) Afterwards, the modality being retrieved is moved towards the mean over the other modality by translating 𝒴 ← 𝒴 − g → ′ \mathcal{Y}\leftarrow\mathcal{Y}-\vec{g}^{\prime} , therefore decreasing the distance of any query point to the retrieved modality, as per Theorem 3.4 . Theorem 3.5 assures us that closing the gap in the direction of g → ′ \vec{g}^{\prime} would not affect performance on any downstream tasks that relies on computing nearest neighbors. In the appendix, we also provide an extension to this algorithm that allows moving in directions that are not perfectly orthogonal to each modality (see Appendix G ). Contrary to previous attempts at closing the gap, our method requires no retraining or finetuning of the models [ 17 , 16 ] , or the training of new ones (such as the prior network in [ 22 , 18 ] ). Our method is also general and does not adhere to a specific setting [ 12 ] - any task using cross modal nearest neighbors could benefit from it.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments
sections.text: (a) CLIP (ViT L-14) on CIFAR10 (b) CLIP (ViT B-16) on CIFAR100 (c) CLIP (ViT B-16) on A-OKVQA (d) SigLIP on A-OKVQA Figure 8 : The zero shot classification accuracy, multiple choice VQA accuracy and robustness under noise η ∼ 𝒩 ⁡ ( 0 , σ 2 ​ I ) \eta\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}I) , on various models and datasets. As predicted by our theory, robustness monotonically increases when the gap is closed while accuracy is maintained. We turn our attention to understanding how well our theory and algorithm work in practice for various real world models and datasets. We follow [ 11 ] and experiment on standard zero shot classification and image-text retrieval tasks. We create embeddings of commonly used, pretrained, multi-modal models using using the openclip library [ 4 ] . To measure robustness, we empirically estimate: R ⁡ ( α ) = 1 K ​ ∑ i = 1 K 1 | 𝒴 | ​ ∑ y ∈ 𝒴 𝟙 NN ​ ( y , 𝒳 + α ⋅ g → ) = NN ​ ( y , ( 𝒳 + ϵ i ) + α ⋅ g → CLOSE \displaystyle R(\alpha)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{i=1}^{K}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{Y}|}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{Y}}\mathds{1}_{\text{NN}(y,\mathcal{X}+\alpha\cdot\vec{g})=\text{NN}(y,(\mathcal{X}+\epsilon_{i})+\alpha\cdot\vec{g}} (12) Where K K is the number of samples of noise, ϵ i ∼ 𝒫 \epsilon_{i}\sim\mathcal{P} is a sample from the noise model 𝒫 \mathcal{P} (such as quantization or gaussian noise) and α ∈ ℝ \alpha\in\mathbb{R} is a scalar controlling the amount of the gap that we close. We set K = 1 K=1 (e.g. when there is a single deterministic quantization) unless stated otherwise. 5.1 Robustness Under Controlled Noise Our first set of experiments attempts to verify our theory and algorithm in the presence of controlled noise added to the embedding space. We add varying degrees of independent Gaussian noise with zero mean and variance σ 2 \sigma^{2} to each text embedding x → ∈ 𝒳 \vec{x}\in\mathcal{X} and translate the text embeddings by α ⋅ g → ′ \alpha\cdot\vec{g}^{\prime} according to our algorithm ( Sec. 4 ). We do this for different values of α \alpha therefore expanding or closing the gap. For each change in the gap, we measure both accuracy and robustness ( Eq. 12 ) averaging over K = 100 K=100 samples of noise. We test our algorithm on various models, in both zero shot classification and visual question answering (VQA) on the A-OKVQA dataset [ 26 ] , following the evaluation protocol of Ghosal et al. [3] for CLIP-like models. Results are displayed in Fig. 8 - when applying our algorithm under Gaussian noise robustness greatly increases when closing the gap across all models and tasks, and greatly decreases when expanding the gap. As noise increases, robustness is lower but still improves when the gap is closed. See Appendix E for similar results on other noise distributions. As predicted by Theorem 3.5 , the zero shot and VQA accuracy do not change when closing the gap in the direction orthogonal to the affine subspace of texts. 5.2 Robustness to Quantization (a) CLIP (ViT L-14) on CIFAR10 (b) CLIP (ViT B-16) on CIFAR100 Figure 9 : CLIP variants are increasingly more robust to quantization as the gap is closed. The gap norm is measured in the non-quantized space. We continue and test our theory and algorithm on noise distributions that apply to real world applications. A setting of uncorrelated noise is that of quantization [ 14 ] . While many forms of model quantizations exist, we limit ourselves to the simple case of post-training quantizing of the embedding vectors alone, a setting relevant to tasks in which the embeddings were calculated in advance e.g. retrieval augmented generation (RAG) [ 38 ] . We close the gap to varying degrees and then quantize the text and image embedding vectors to different numbers of intervals between a constant range of [ − 3 , 3 ] \left[-3,3\right] (as all embeddings are on the unit hypersphere), and measure robustness. Empirically, we find that since quantization noise does not always have zero mean, it is better to close the gap until the gap is minimized in the quantized embedding space rather than the original one. Figure 9 displays results for these experiments. As can be seen, robustness is greatly improved when closing the gap before quantizing the embedding vectors. 5.3 Robustness to Rephrasing We now turn our attention to text rephrasings - noise that is added in the input space rather than embedding space - which we’ve investigated thus far. We find that in this setting our theoretical assumptions do not hold - specifically, the noise in the embedding space that results from the rephrasing has non-zero mean and tends to lie entirely within the text subspace, with little to no variance in the direction of the gap (and see Appendix F ). This is not surprising as models that are trained on large datasets are expected to be invariant to various input noises, such as text rephrasing. We find that our algorithm can indeed be used for such cases. For each question in the A-OKVQA dataset, we simulate a sample of random noise by sampling 3 random wrong answers and a random correct answer, exact details are provided in Appendix F . Since in this setting the answers are randomly selected, we focus on measuring accuracy under noise instead of robustness, while closing the gap using our algorithm. Results are presented in Fig. 10 - accuracy under rephrasings greatly increases when the gap is closed using our algorithm, while clean accuracy is unaffected. (a) CLIP (ViT B-16) (b) SigLIP Figure 10 : We apply rephrasing noise to textual inputs on the A-OKVQA dataset, and measure average accuracy and rephrase accuracy in the noisy setting over K = 500 K=500 samples of wrong and correct answers for each question. Models are increasingly more accurate once the gap is closed, without change in clean accuracy, even though this setting is far from our theoretical assumptions.

sections.heading: 6 Discussion
sections.text: In this paper, we have attempted to provide a comprehensive theory for the formation of an orthogonal gap in multi-modal models. Specifically we showed that when initializing with tight clusters, minimizing the contrastive loss will lead to solutions where a global gap vector separates the two modalities and that this vector will be orthogonal to both modalities. We continued to examine the effect of such a gap in the context of robustness. We prove that in this context, the gap is indeed a bug - as the modality gap increases, the consistency of the retrieval when applying subtle variations to the embedding space is decreased. Following this theoretical insight, we presented a simple and computationally inexpensive algorithm that improves robustness with hardly any reduction in clean accuracy. Our algorithm could easily be implemented as a post processing step when using multi-modal model embeddings. Finally, we began examining the effect of our theory and algorithm in the context of real noise, such as quantization and text rephrasing. We view our experiments as a hint to the potential of our algorithm and encourage further investigation as to settings of noise in which our simple algorithm could improve downstream performance.
